The proposal to abolish homework in primary schools is a well-intentioned but deeply misguided one. While children need time to play and rest, a modest amount of daily homework is not a burden; it is a vital bridge between the classroom and lasting learning. Eliminating it would weaken the academic foundations and personal habits that young pupils urgently need.

The most immediate benefit of daily homework is that it reinforces the reading and arithmetic skills taught in class. Young children do not master phonics or number bonds after a single lesson; they need repeated, distributed practice to move new knowledge into long-term memory. A short daily reading session allows a child to apply decoding strategies independently, building fluency and confidence. Likewise, ten minutes of arithmetic practice, whether simple addition or multiplication tables, consolidates mental maths in a way that a busy classroom timetable cannot guarantee. Without this regular reinforcement, skills learned on Monday can easily fade by Friday, forcing teachers to spend valuable class time reteaching rather than advancing.

Homework also cultivates the independent work habits that become essential in secondary school. When a primary pupil sits down to complete a worksheet or read a chapter alone, they learn to manage their time, follow instructions without constant prompting, and take responsibility for their own output. A child who has never been asked to complete a task at home will find the sudden expectation of independent study in secondary school overwhelming. Primary homework, even in small doses, builds the self-discipline and routine that allow older students to plan essays, revise for exams, and meet deadlines without relying on a teacher hovering nearby.

Finally, homework serves as a crucial window for parents into their child’s education. When a parent sits beside a child struggling with a spelling list or a simple division problem, they gain direct insight into what is being taught and where their child may need support. This involvement allows parents to reinforce learning at home, praise effort, and raise concerns early, rather than discovering difficulties only at a parents’ evening months later. Homework turns the abstract idea of “school” into a visible, shared activity, strengthening the partnership between home and classroom.

Abolishing homework would not protect childhood; it would rob children of the repetition, responsibility, and parental connection that make learning stick. Primary schools should keep daily homework, keeping it short and purposeful, so that every child can build the habits and skills that will carry them forward.

The proposal to abolish homework in primary schools is a well-intentioned but deeply misguided one, for it would rob young learners of a crucial bridge between the classroom and lasting mastery. Daily homework is not mere busywork; it is an essential tool for cementing the foundational skills in reading and arithmetic that all future learning depends upon. A child who spends twenty minutes practising multiplication tables or reading aloud at home is consolidating neural pathways that a crowded school day simply cannot fully secure. Class time introduces a concept, but it is the repeated, focused practice at home that transforms fragile understanding into automatic recall. Without this daily reinforcement, many children would return each morning having forgotten much of the previous day’s lesson, forcing teachers to spend valuable time reteaching rather than moving forward.

Beyond academic consolidation, homework plays an indispensable role in nurturing the independent work habits that secondary school demands. In primary school, children are closely guided by a single teacher; in secondary school, they must manage assignments from multiple subjects, meet deadlines, and study alone. A gradual introduction to daily homework teaches a child to organise a small amount of time, resist the temptation to stop when a task feels challenging, and take responsibility for completing and returning work. A ten-year-old who has learned to sit down unprompted and finish a short maths sheet is far better prepared for the self-discipline of secondary education than one who has never been asked to work outside the classroom. Abolishing homework would send children into this more demanding environment without the very habits they need to survive it.

Finally, homework serves as a vital window through which parents can observe their child’s learning. A parent who listens to a child read, or checks a page of sums, gains a clear and immediate sense of what is being taught and where their child might be struggling. This involvement is not intrusive but collaborative; it allows parents to praise progress, notice confusion early, and communicate intelligently with teachers. Without homework, parents are left guessing about the curriculum and their child’s daily experience. The small amount of time homework requires is a modest price for this informed partnership, and to abolish it would be to sever one of the strongest links between home and school.

In cities worldwide, public transport remains a vital artery, yet the fares charged to use it may do more harm than good. Eliminating fares entirely would not be a reckless giveaway but a strategic investment, yielding benefits that far outweigh lost ticket revenue.

First, the very act of collecting fares is a substantial financial burden. Transit operators spend heavily on fareboxes, ticket vending machines, smart card systems, payment processing, and the staff needed to enforce and maintain them. These administrative costs consume a significant share of every dollar collected. By abolishing fares, agencies could redirect these funds toward more frequent buses, extended hours, cleaner stations, and better maintenance, which are direct service improvements that riders feel immediately. The apparent loss of fare revenue is partly illusory, offset by the removal of an expensive collection apparatus.

Second, free public transport would lure drivers out of their cars for short urban trips. When a bus or tram ride costs nothing, the calculation changes dramatically: a quick errand, a commute across town, or a journey to a restaurant no longer invites comparison with the price of petrol and parking. As more people choose transit, city streets become less choked with single-occupancy vehicles. Reduced congestion speeds up buses themselves, creating a virtuous cycle of reliability and attractiveness. Cleaner air, lower emissions, and safer streets are natural by-products.

Third, and most importantly, free fares would dismantle a barrier that disproportionately harms low-income residents. For those living paycheck to paycheck, even a modest fare can mean choosing between transport and food, medicine, or school supplies. Free transit would open access to jobs that were previously unreachable, enable reliable attendance at medical appointments, and connect families to libraries, parks, and community services. This is not charity; it is the removal of a regressive toll on mobility, allowing everyone to participate fully in the economic and social life of the city.

The cost of doing nothing is measured in wasted administrative spending, gridlocked streets, and human potential trapped by poverty. Free public transport is not a utopian dream but a practical policy that would make cities fairer, faster, and more efficient for all.

The Case for Remote-First Office Work

Office jobs should default to remote arrangements because doing so benefits employees, employers, and the broader economy. By removing the daily commute, companies give workers back hundreds of hours each year while also expanding their hiring reach and cutting major real estate costs.

The most immediate gain is reclaimed time. The average American commuter spends nearly an hour per day traveling to and from work, adding up to roughly 200 hours annually. Under a remote-first model, that time can be redirected toward exercise, family, rest, or additional focused work. Many employees report that they use former commuting hours to start their day more calmly or to complete deep-work tasks before household distractions begin. This often boosts productivity rather than reducing it, since workers can align their schedules with their natural energy peaks.

Remote default also removes geographic barriers to hiring. A company no longer needs to limit itself to candidates who live within a reasonable drive of a headquarters. This is especially valuable for specialized roles, such as software engineers, data scientists, or multilingual customer support staff, where local talent may be scarce. For example, a tech firm in a small city could hire an experienced AI researcher in another state or country instead of waiting months for a local applicant. Access to a broader talent pool also increases diversity of background and perspective, which can strengthen problem-solving and innovation.

Finally, businesses can save significantly on real estate. Office space, utilities, maintenance, and furniture represent major fixed costs. Research from Global Workplace Analytics suggests employers can save around $11,000 per year for each employee who works remotely half the time. A 100-person company could redirect over $1 million annually into higher salaries, employee benefits, or research and development. These savings make remote work not only a lifestyle perk but a competitive financial strategy.

Remote-first office work is not merely a pandemic-era compromise. It is a practical default that returns time to employees, widens the talent market, and frees capital for innovation. Companies that embrace this model position themselves to attract better talent and invest more wisely.

In cities around the world, public transport is expected to pay for itself through fares, but this assumption overlooks the hidden costs of charging for every ride. Eliminating fares on urban buses, trams and metros would be a strategic investment in efficiency, mobility and equity.

First, fare collection is expensive. Transit agencies must buy and maintain ticketing machines, handle cash, run payment systems, and employ staff to inspect tickets and pursue fare evasion. These administrative burdens consume a significant share of operating budgets, sometimes approaching the revenue fares actually generate. Removing fares would let agencies redirect that money into more frequent service, cleaner vehicles and expanded routes—improvements that benefit all passengers more than a cumbersome payment apparatus.

Second, free public transport would encourage drivers to leave their cars for short trips. When a bus or tram costs nothing, a two-kilometre journey that once involved fuel, parking and a ticket becomes the obvious choice. As more people choose transit for errands and commutes, city streets would carry fewer private vehicles. This would reduce congestion, shorten travel times for essential traffic, cut emissions and make streets safer for pedestrians and cyclists. The congestion relieved by free transit is itself an economic gain.

Finally, abolishing fares directly tackles transport poverty. Low-income residents often spend a disproportionate share of their income on getting to work, medical appointments and schools. For many, a daily bus pass is a genuine barrier, forcing difficult choices between mobility and other necessities. Free transit would widen access to jobs, services and social connections, reducing the isolation that entrenches poverty. It is a practical form of inclusion, delivered simply by opening the doors.

The objections to free transit usually focus on cost, but they ignore the costs we already pay: collecting fares, congestion from avoidable driving, and the human cost of restricted mobility. By removing fares, cities can build transport systems that are more efficient, more widely used and more just.

The default office job is a relic of the Industrial Age, not a necessity of the Information Age. Making remote work the default would return hundreds of hours to employees annually, expand companies’ access to talent, and redirect significant real estate spending into innovation and wages.

First, remote work gives employees back their commutes. The average American spends roughly 55 minutes per day traveling to and from work—about 230 hours per year. Under a remote default, those hours become flexible capital. An employee could use them for exercise, family care, or leisure, reducing burnout and improving retention. Alternatively, employees can reinvest that time into deep, uninterrupted work. A Stanford study of a Chinese travel agency found that remote workers were 13 percent more productive, largely because they started earlier, took shorter breaks, and worked with fewer distractions. The commute, not the office, is often what drains energy.

Second, remote hiring removes geographical limits. When a company stops requiring physical presence in one city, it can recruit from an entire country—or the world. A firm in San Francisco no longer competes only for local engineers but can hire a specialist in rural Texas, a designer in Toronto, or a data scientist in Madrid. This wider pool increases diversity of background and thought while reducing the salary inflation caused by overconcentration in a few coastal metros. For example, GitLab and Automattic have built fully remote workforces of thousands across dozens of countries, accessing skills unavailable in any single headquarters city.

Third, companies save significantly on real estate. Global Workplace Analytics estimates that each half-time remote worker saves an employer about $11,000 annually in office costs. A company with 1,000 remote-first employees could save $11 million per year—enough to fund a serious R&D program or provide meaningful raises. Instead of paying premium rent for underused space, businesses can invest in product development, security infrastructure, and competitive compensation.

Reclaiming commute hours, tapping talent without borders, and converting rent into research and wages: the case for remote-first office work is not about convenience but about economic rationality and human capital. Businesses that default to remote work will be leaner, more innovative, and better staffed for the future of work.

**The Indispensable Core: Why Nuclear Power is Vital for Deep Decarbonisation**

Achieving a truly decarbonised electricity grid requires a clear-eyed assessment of available technologies. While renewable sources like wind and solar are crucial, a reliable and low-carbon future is unattainable without the unique attributes of nuclear power. Its ability to provide firm, clean energy makes it an indispensable cornerstone of any serious climate strategy.

The primary challenge of a renewables-heavy grid is intermittency. Solar and wind generation are contingent on meteorological conditions, creating significant variability and the need for massive energy storage or backup. Nuclear power, conversely, offers a stable, dispatchable baseload output irrespective of weather or time of day. This high capacity factor, consistently above 90% for U.S. fleets, provides the essential firm power that stabilises the grid, complementing and enabling greater penetration of variable renewables without risking blackouts.

Furthermore, when considering lifecycle emissions, nuclear power stands alongside the best low-carbon technologies. Assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) consistently show the median lifecycle emissions of nuclear power to be around 12 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour. This is comparable to wind power and significantly lower than solar photovoltaic, and an order of magnitude less than even the most efficient natural gas plants. Its immense energy density ensures that the entire process, from uranium mining to plant decommissioning, has a minimal carbon footprint.

Finally, nuclear power’s compact land-use requirements present a decisive advantage. A typical 1,000-megawatt nuclear reactor requires approximately one square mile of land. To generate the same annual energy output, a wind farm would require hundreds of square miles, and a solar farm even more. This immense spatial footprint leads to greater habitat disruption and transmission challenges. Nuclear’s high power density minimises environmental intrusion, preserving land for ecosystems, agriculture, and other human needs.

In conclusion, dismissing nuclear power is to forfeit a proven tool in the fight against climate change. Its grid-stabilising reliability, minimal lifecycle emissions, and efficient land use make it not merely an option, but a fundamental necessity for a sustainable and resilient energy future.

The proposition of mandatory age verification for social media is a superficially appealing but ultimately flawed solution to a complex problem. While the goal of protecting minors is laudable, the implementation of such measures would inflict significant collateral damage, eroding fundamental rights while offering only a false sense of security. A robust argument against this mandate rests on its profound threats to privacy, its practical ineffectiveness, and its inequitable impact on society.

First, mandatory verification would necessitate the creation of a digital identity infrastructure, a veritable treasure trove of personal data. Requiring government-issued IDs or biometric data to access social platforms would effectively end anonymous browsing and speech, forces that are crucial for whistleblowers, activists, and vulnerable individuals seeking support. This centralization of sensitive data creates an irresistible target for hackers and expands the surveillance capabilities of both corporations and governments, fundamentally altering the open nature of the internet.

Second, the proposed system is unlikely to be effective. A determined teenager can easily circumvent age gates by using a parent’s credentials, borrowing an ID, or utilizing readily available VPNs to appear to be in a different jurisdiction. Consequently, such laws would primarily punish privacy-conscious adults rather than deter tech-savvy youth. The result is a security theater that does little to address the underlying issues of online harm, such as algorithmic amplification of harmful content or a lack of digital literacy.

Finally, this mandate creates an unequal burden. It would erect a barrier to entry for low-income individuals, the elderly, and those without stable housing who may lack the necessary identification documents. Ironically, these are often the populations who rely most on social media for community connection and essential information. A policy that disenfranchises these groups to address a problem it cannot solve is not a solution but a new problem in itself. Ultimately, the collateral damage to privacy, free expression, and equity far outweighs the marginal benefits of a system built on a flawed premise.

While proponents of mandatory age verification for social media platforms present it as a straightforward solution to protect minors, such a policy is a misguided approach that would sacrifice fundamental rights, prove ineffective, and create new inequalities. The potential harms of this proposition far outweigh its intended benefits.

The most immediate consequence of mandatory verification is a severe erosion of individual privacy. To verify age, platforms would be forced to collect sensitive, government-issued identification from all users. This would create a centralized honeypot of personal data, making it a prime target for hackers and data breaches. Furthermore, it would effectively end anonymous online speech, a cornerstone of free expression that is vital for whistleblowers, activists, and individuals exploring their identities without fear of real-world repercussions. This chilling effect on speech is an unacceptable price for a false sense of security.

Beyond privacy, the effectiveness of such measures is highly doubtful. A tech-savvy teenager, determined to access these platforms, can easily bypass verification through a simple web search for a parent’s ID, a borrowed card, or readily available VPNs. The system would create a digital cat-and-mouse game, where only the most naive are deterred. This creates a false sense of security for parents and policymakers while driving minors towards unregulated, and potentially more dangerous, corners of the internet.

Finally, the burden of this policy would fall unequally on the population. Mandatory verification would disenfranchise vulnerable groups, including the elderly, low-income individuals, and those without stable housing who may lack the required identification documents. A significant portion of the population does not possess a passport or driver’s license, effectively barring them from these essential communication platforms. This digital divide would disproportionately silence marginalized voices, undermining the very goal of a safe and inclusive digital public square.

In conclusion, mandatory age verification is a policy of high cost and low reward. It would fatally compromise user privacy, be easily circumvented by the very demographic it seeks to protect, and create an unequal system that excludes vulnerable citizens. Instead of this blunt instrument, resources should be directed toward robust digital literacy programs, better parental controls developed in partnership with tech companies, and improved content moderation. These solutions offer a path to online safety without sacrificing our fundamental rights.

While critics often decry standardized tests as biased barriers, abandoning them would actually undermine equity and academic readiness in university admissions. A common test remains one of the few tools that can compare students fairly across vastly different educational contexts, and its removal would deepen existing inequalities rather than reduce them.

A standardized test provides a level playing field for applicants from diverse educational backgrounds. High school grading standards vary enormously between schools, districts, and even countries; an “A” at one institution may reflect far less rigorous expectations than a “B” at another. Standardized tests, by contrast, present the same content, timing, and scoring to every student, creating a common benchmark. For a talented student at an under-resourced or lesser-known school, a strong test score can signal potential that inflated or inconsistent grades might obscure. Without such a measure, admissions officers must rely on grades whose meaning shifts from one transcript to the next, disadvantaging students whose schools lack reputational capital.

Moreover, eliminating standardized tests would exacerbate existing inequalities in admissions. In their absence, universities would lean more heavily on grade point averages, personal essays, recommendation letters, and extracurricular activities—all of which are profoundly shaped by family wealth and school resources. Affluent applicants can hire essay coaches, enroll in Advanced Placement or International Baccalaureate programs at well-funded schools, and pursue expensive extracurriculars that impress admissions committees. Students from low-income or rural backgrounds often lack these opportunities. A standardized test, while imperfect, offers a relatively inexpensive way for a disadvantaged student to demonstrate academic ability independent of such advantages. Removing it removes one of the few objective measures that can counterbalance privilege.

Finally, standardized tests possess meaningful predictive validity for first-year university success. Research consistently shows that test scores predict first-year grade point average and retention, and they add incremental predictive power beyond high school grades alone. High school grades reflect effort and persistence but are increasingly subject to grade inflation and inconsistency across schools. Standardized tests capture reasoning, reading comprehension, and quantitative skills under uniform conditions, which are directly relevant to college coursework. Used together, grades and test scores forecast student success more accurately than either measure alone, helping universities identify applicants likely to thrive academically.

Rather than discarding standardized tests, universities should use them as one contextualized factor alongside grades and socioeconomic background. Doing so preserves a common yardstick, guards against inequity, and strengthens the selection of students prepared for university rigor.

In the quiet machinery of daily commerce, the physical banknote remains a quiet guarantor of autonomy and continuity, and its steady circulation should not be surrendered to the allure of digital convenience alone. Cash is not merely a relic; it is a resilient public utility that protects individuals when the invisible systems around them falter.

Consider first the resilience of cash in moments of infrastructural collapse. A severe storm, a regional blackout, or a targeted cyberattack can silence card readers, disable mobile payment apps, and freeze online banking portals in an instant. When the power grid fails or network signals vanish, a twenty-pound note still buys bread, fuel, and medicine. Cash operates without servers, authentication protocols, or electricity, making it the only universally functional medium of exchange during emergencies. This infrastructural independence is not a nostalgic luxury but a practical safeguard, ensuring that communities are not left helpless precisely when they are most vulnerable.

Equally significant is the unique anonymity that cash provides. Every digital transaction, however small, leaves a trace—a timestamped record held by banks, payment processors, and merchants. Cash, by contrast, is the sole mainstream payment method that generates no transactional ledger. It allows individuals to purchase sensitive items, donate to causes, or simply live without the quiet scrutiny of data aggregators. This anonymity is not about facilitating wrongdoing; it is about preserving a sphere of private choice in an age of pervasive surveillance. The ability to spend without being watched is a fundamental liberty, and cash remains its most tangible instrument.

Finally, cash is indispensable to those whom the digital economy too often leaves behind. Millions of elderly citizens, unfamiliar or uncomfortable with smartphones and banking apps, rely on notes and coins for their weekly shopping and household bills. Likewise, unbanked individuals—those without access to formal financial institutions—have no practical alternative to cash for receiving wages, paying rent, or saving modest sums. For these groups, the push toward a cashless society is not progress but exclusion. Maintaining a robust circulation of physical currency is therefore not a retreat from innovation; it is a commitment to an inclusive, resilient, and free society.

**In Defense of Standardized Tests in University Admissions**

Some argue that universities should abandon standardized tests in admissions, but doing so would weaken fairness, deepen inequality, and reduce the ability to predict student success. A well-designed standardized test remains a vital tool.

A common standardized test provides a level playing field for applicants from diverse educational backgrounds. High school grades are shaped by wildly different curricula, grading standards, and resources. A 4.0 from an under-resourced rural school may reflect far less exposure to advanced material than a 3.5 from an elite private academy. A standardized test offers a uniform benchmark, measuring core academic skills independent of local context. This allows admissions officers to identify talented students who might otherwise be overlooked due to grade inflation or deflation, giving applicants from varied schools a fair common yardstick.

Its absence would exacerbate existing inequalities in the admissions process. Without standardized tests, universities would rely more heavily on essays, interviews, extracurricular activities, and recommendation letters—all of which are strongly correlated with family wealth and social capital. Affluent applicants can hire essay coaches, pursue expensive activities, and secure polished letters from well-connected mentors. Grades, too, favor students in well-funded schools with extensive Advanced Placement or International Baccalaureate offerings. Removing an objective test would eliminate one of the few metrics through which a motivated student from a modest background can directly demonstrate academic ability, tilting the process further toward privilege.

Finally, standardized tests possess meaningful predictive validity compared to high school grades in forecasting first-year university success. While grades capture sustained effort, they are not comparable across schools. Research consistently shows that standardized test scores add incremental predictive power beyond grades alone, especially when the two are combined. Tests provide a consistent measure of the reading, writing, and quantitative skills required for college-level work. Students with strong scores but modest grades often succeed, while very low scores can signal readiness gaps that grades may conceal.

Abandoning standardized tests would remove a democratizing common measure, shift weight toward privilege-saturated factors, and weaken the ability to forecast academic success. Universities should reform tests to reduce bias, not discard them.

The case for a four-day working week as national policy no longer rests on idealism alone; it is grounded in a growing body of evidence that shorter hours can benefit workers, employers, and the wider economy. By rethinking our attachment to the five-day grind, we can build a more productive, healthier, and fairer society.

First, trials across various industries have consistently shown that employees can maintain, and sometimes even improve, their output when working four days instead of five. The reason is simple: a compressed schedule forces organisations to eliminate low-value tasks, shorten unnecessary meetings, and focus on what truly matters. Workers, knowing they have a longer weekend to recover, often bring sharper concentration and greater urgency to their four days on the job. The result is that the same volume of work gets done, but with less wasted time. This challenges the outdated assumption that hours spent at a desk are the best measure of contribution.

Second, a better-rested workforce takes significantly less sick leave. Chronic stress, burnout, and exhaustion are major drivers of both physical and mental illness, and they are often direct products of the relentless five-day cycle. A three-day weekend provides genuine time for recovery, family responsibilities, and personal health, reducing the accumulation of stress that leads to long-term absenteeism. Employers therefore gain not only from reduced sick days but also from lower presenteeism, where exhausted employees show up but perform poorly. Healthier workers are more engaged, more loyal, and less likely to require costly medical interventions, saving businesses and public health systems money in the long run.

Finally, adopting a four-day week as national policy would help spread available work across more people, creating new jobs. In many sectors, the total volume of work is not infinite, yet it is currently concentrated in the hands of a smaller number of overworked employees. By reducing the standard working week, employers who need continuous coverage or high output would be compelled to hire additional staff to fill the gap. This redistribution of hours would lower unemployment, reduce reliance on welfare, and give more individuals the dignity and security of a paid job without requiring any single person to sacrifice their health or family life.

In short, the four-day working week is not a retreat from productivity but a smarter way to organise it. The evidence from trials, the benefits to public health, and the potential for job creation all point in the same direction. It is time for national policy to catch up with what forward-thinking employers have already discovered: that less can truly be more.

The proposition that space-exploration funding should be diverted to ocean research rests on a mistaken assumption of a simple budgetary trade-off. In reality, the two fields are supported through largely distinct financial and institutional channels. Space programmes are typically funded by dedicated space agencies and their associated legislative appropriations, while ocean research is supported by oceanographic and atmospheric agencies, universities, and separate international bodies. Money cut from a planetary mission or a deep-space telescope does not automatically reappear in the account of a marine research institute. Because these budgets are negotiated independently and often involve long-term international commitments, the idea that reducing one will reliably enlarge the other is illusory. Redirecting funds would more likely shrink overall scientific capacity than produce a neat transfer to the oceans.

Secondly, far from competing with ocean research, space technology is already one of its most powerful tools. Satellite observation, a central component of space programmes, provides the continuous, global measurements that modern oceanography depends on. Altimetry satellites track sea-level rise; gravimetric missions measure ocean mass and currents; radiometers record sea-surface temperature; and ocean-colour sensors monitor phytoplankton and marine ecosystems. Without this space-based infrastructure, oceanographers would be forced to rely on sparse ship tracks and scattered buoys, losing the synoptic view needed to understand climate change, fisheries, and ocean circulation. Cutting space funding in the name of ocean research would therefore damage the very observational foundation upon which much of that research now rests.

Thirdly, space programmes generate spillover benefits that are uniquely broad and deep. The extreme engineering demands of spaceflight have driven advances in miniaturised electronics, solar power, imaging sensors, materials science, software, and communications. Satellite navigation alone underpins global logistics, agriculture, financial timing, and emergency response. Medical imaging, water purification, and even memory-foam products trace their origins to space investment. While ocean research also produces valuable knowledge, the cross-industry catalytic effect of space exploration is exceptional in both scale and variety. Diverting a significant share of space funding would therefore sacrifice a disproportionately productive engine of technological innovation for an uncertain and structurally separate gain.

The argument that space-exploration funding should be diverted to ocean research rests on a mistaken assumption that these two scientific enterprises compete for the same pot of money. In practice, their budgets are largely distinct, allocated through separate agencies, committees, and policy priorities. Space exploration is typically funded by national space agencies and their planetary science divisions, while ocean research draws on environmental, fisheries, and earth-science budgets. A cut to a Mars rover programme does not automatically reappear as new funding for deep-sea submersibles or marine ecosystem surveys; the appropriations processes are neither linked nor interchangeable. Consequently, framing the choice as a direct trade-off is illusory, and redirecting funds would more likely diminish space capabilities without producing any guaranteed increase in ocean science.

Moreover, space research is already one of the most powerful tools available to oceanographers. Satellite observation, developed and maintained through space programmes, supplies continuous global measurements of sea-surface temperature, ocean colour, salinity, winds, currents, and sea-level rise. Missions using radar altimetry, gravimetry, and multispectral imaging allow scientists to track phenomena that would be impossible to monitor comprehensively from ships or buoys alone, from large-scale circulation patterns to the melting of polar ice sheets. Far from competing with ocean research, space-based infrastructure is integral to modern marine science. Reducing space funding would therefore weaken, not strengthen, our ability to understand the oceans.

Finally, space programmes have a uniquely high level of spillover into other industries, generating benefits that extend far beyond exploration itself. The extreme demands of spaceflight—miniaturization, reliability, energy efficiency, and autonomous operation—have driven advances in computing, telecommunications, materials science, robotics, medical devices, and Earth observation. Technologies originally developed for space missions now underpin GPS navigation, weather forecasting, disaster response, and global communications. While ocean research also produces valuable knowledge, its industrial spillovers have not matched the breadth and economic scale of those flowing from space investment. Redirecting funding away from space would therefore sacrifice a proven engine of cross-sector innovation for a false promise of budgetary gain.

Those who call for the phasing out of zoos often overlook the quiet miracles that occur behind their enclosures. Far from being mere displays, modern zoos function as arks for biodiversity, as classrooms for compassion, and as laboratories for lifesaving science. To dismantle them would be to sever some of the most effective lifelines available to endangered species.

Perhaps the most compelling argument for preserving zoos is their indispensable role in captive breeding programmes. Species such as the Arabian oryx, the California condor, and Przewalski’s horse have been pulled back from the very brink of extinction solely because zoos maintained genetically viable populations and coordinated meticulous reintroduction efforts. In a world of accelerating habitat loss and climate disruption, wild populations can vanish with terrifying speed. Zoos provide a managed safety net, preserving genetic diversity that would otherwise be lost forever and offering the possibility of restoring species to the wild once threats have been mitigated. Phasing out zoos would close the door on this proven conservation tool at a moment when it is needed most.

Equally vital is the unique power of direct contact between the public and living animals. No nature documentary, however stunning, can replicate the transformative experience of locking eyes with a gorilla or hearing a lion’s breath. Such encounters forge emotional connections that abstract statistics cannot. Children who meet a rescued sea turtle or watch a keeper feed a red panda are far more likely to grow into adults who support habitat protection, donate to conservation charities, and make environmentally responsible choices. Zoos turn passive awareness into active advocacy. Removing this bridge between urban humanity and the natural world would risk leaving conservation as a distant, intellectual concern rather than a deeply felt personal commitment.

Finally, the veterinary expertise honed within zoos has yielded profound benefits for wild animal populations. Zoo veterinarians routinely develop anaesthetic protocols, diagnostic techniques, and surgical procedures on animals that can then be applied in field conditions. For instance, methods for immobilising large carnivores, treating amphibian chytrid fungus, and performing health assessments on free-ranging primates were pioneered or refined in zoological settings. When disease outbreaks strike wild herds or when injured animals are discovered in national parks, wildlife veterinarians rely on knowledge generated in zoo hospitals. Closing zoos would not only halt this research but also dismantle a network of skilled professionals who stand ready to respond to wildlife emergencies.

In sum, phasing out zoos would be a dangerous act of ecological negligence. We should reform zoos where necessary, but we must not abandon them, for they are not prisons but lifelines.

The imperative to decarbonise electricity while meeting rising demand cannot be met by variable renewables alone. Nuclear power’s weather-independent output, exceptionally low lifecycle emissions, and minimal land footprint make it an indispensable pillar of a reliable zero-carbon system.

First, nuclear provides firm, dispatchable baseload generation. Reactors in the United States routinely achieve capacity factors above 90 per cent, compared with roughly 35 per cent for wind and 25 per cent for solar photovoltaics. Because reactor output does not depend on wind speed, cloud cover or season, nuclear directly compensates for renewable intermittency during calm, cloudy “dunkelflaute” periods and seasonal storage gaps. Modelling by Jenkins et al. and Sepulveda et al. in *Joule* shows that firm low-carbon resources substantially reduce the costs of deeply decarbonised grids by limiting the need for massive storage and overbuilding.

Second, lifecycle assessments demonstrate that nuclear is among the lowest-carbon sources available. The IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report estimates a median of 12 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for nuclear, essentially equal to wind at 11 grams and well below utility-scale solar PV at 48 grams. More recent UNECE analysis places nuclear at 5.1–6.0 grams CO₂ per kilowatt-hour, comparable to or lower than wind. These figures include uranium mining, enrichment, construction, operation and decommissioning, confirming nuclear is not a high-carbon compromise but a genuinely low-carbon technology.

Third, nuclear’s land-use requirements are dramatically smaller than those of wind and solar. UNECE life-cycle assessments report land occupation of approximately 0.5 square metres per megawatt-hour for nuclear, compared with roughly 5–30 for solar PV and 8–55 for wind, depending on siting. A single gigawatt-scale reactor can operate on one to four square kilometres, whereas equivalent annual generation from dispersed renewables may require hundreds of square kilometres, fragmenting habitats and lengthening transmission corridors. This compactness is critical where land is ecologically or agriculturally valuable.

Nuclear power therefore complements renewables by providing stability when weather fails, matching their low emissions, and sparing land. A credible decarbonisation strategy cannot afford to exclude it.

The proposal that every child should be taught programming from the age of six is well intentioned but ultimately misguided. While digital competence is increasingly important, forcing coding into the earliest years of schooling ignores how young children learn best and places unrealistic demands on schools. A more thoughtful approach would reserve formal programming instruction for later in a child’s education.

The early years of education are most effectively spent building a strong foundation in language, number sense, and imaginative play. At six, children are still developing the oral vocabulary, listening skills, and social awareness that underpin all later academic work. Rich storytelling, counting games, building with blocks, and pretend play teach children to sequence events, follow rules, and solve problems in concrete, meaningful ways. These experiences develop the very cognitive habits that programming will eventually require, but they do so through developmentally appropriate activity. Replacing such play with screen-based coding lessons risks narrowing the curriculum and depriving children of the hands-on exploration their brains need most.

Furthermore, the rapid pace of change in programming tools and technologies means that skills learned at a young age are likely to become outdated long before a child is old enough to apply them. A six-year-old who masters a particular block-based platform or a simplified language will not necessarily be better prepared for the professional programming environments of a decade later. Languages, frameworks, and interfaces evolve constantly, and early exposure to one tool offers little lasting advantage. The valuable underlying logic of programming can be taught just as effectively through puzzles, mathematics, and structured play, without tying a child’s learning to software that will soon be obsolete.

Finally, the current shortage of qualified teachers makes it unrealistic to expect that all schools will be able to provide high-quality coding instruction to every child. Many primary school teachers have no formal training in computer science, and expecting them to teach programming confidently is unfair to both educators and students. Without expert guidance, coding lessons often become shallow, recipe-following exercises that frustrate children rather than inspire them. Schools in affluent areas may hire specialist staff, but schools with fewer resources will struggle, widening existing educational inequalities. Mandating coding for all six-year-olds would therefore promise an opportunity that many schools simply cannot deliver.

Programming is a valuable skill, but it does not belong at the centre of early childhood education. A wiser policy would protect the early years for language, play, and foundational numeracy, and introduce coding later, when children are developmentally ready and schools are genuinely equipped to teach it well.

The most immediate and visible benefit of banning private cars from city centres is the liberation of vast tracts of street space that were once surrendered to moving and parked vehicles. A single private car, often carrying just one occupant, occupies roughly the same area as eight to ten pedestrians or several bicycles, yet for most of the day it sits idle, consuming valuable urban land. Removing these vehicles allows this space to be reallocated to uses that serve far more people. Wide, unobstructed pavements can replace narrow, crowded walkways, enabling pedestrians to move safely and comfortably. Dedicated, protected cycle lanes can be installed without squeezing other road users, encouraging a shift to active travel. Furthermore, the reclaimed space can host café terraces, market stalls, green planters, benches and public art, transforming sterile traffic corridors into vibrant social and commercial arenas. The city centre ceases to be a place one drives through and becomes a place one chooses to linger in.

The environmental case for such bans is powerfully supported by empirical evidence showing rapid and dramatic improvements in both air quality and noise pollution. Private cars are a dominant source of urban nitrogen dioxide, particulate matter and carbon monoxide, as well as the low-frequency engine and tyre roar that forms the constant acoustic backdrop of most cities. Where bans have been introduced, monitoring stations have consistently recorded steep declines in these pollutants within months, not years. For instance, following the introduction of stringent low-emission or car-free zones in cities such as Madrid, Paris and Oslo, concentrations of nitrogen dioxide fell by up to thirty to forty percent in the affected central districts, while average daytime noise levels dropped by several decibels. Because decibel scales are logarithmic, even a reduction of three decibels represents a halving of sound energy. These are not marginal gains but transformative shifts in the sensory environment, delivering immediate public health benefits, particularly for children, the elderly and those with respiratory conditions.

Perhaps the most counterintuitive finding is that removing private cars does not strangle city-centre commerce; it revitalises it. The initial fear among some retailers is that customers will vanish if they cannot park directly outside a shop. Yet the evidence from cities that have pedestrianised or restricted car access consistently shows the opposite: retail footfall increases, sometimes substantially. This is because people on foot or on bicycles visit more frequently, stay longer and spend more per square metre of street space than drivers, who tend to make a single, hurried trip. Freed from traffic danger and noise, shoppers browse more leisurely, discover new businesses and return more often. Cities such as Copenhagen, Ghent and Pontevedra have all reported rising footfall and commercial turnover in their car-free cores, demonstrating that when a city is designed for people rather than vehicles, economic vitality follows.

The case for a four-day working week as national policy has moved from fringe idealism to evidence-based common sense. Trials across sectors demonstrate that shorter hours need not mean lower output; in fact, they often sharpen focus and eliminate wasted time. Adopting this model nationally would benefit workers, employers, and the wider economy through sustained productivity, reduced absence, and greater job creation.

First, the fear that fewer hours automatically means less work is contradicted by real-world experiments. In trials from Iceland to Japan, employees working four days maintained or even increased their output by cutting meetings, reducing distractions, and concentrating effort into more efficient bursts. Microsoft Japan reported a 40 per cent rise in productivity during a four-day week trial, while UK pilot programmes found revenue held steady or grew. When people know their time is shorter, they prioritise ruthlessly and avoid presenteeism, proving that output is a matter of intensity, not mere clocked hours.

Second, a better-rested workforce takes less sick leave. Chronic overwork drives stress, burnout, and physical illness, all of which cost employers and public health systems dearly. A four-day week gives employees a full extra day for recovery, medical appointments, exercise, and family responsibilities, reducing the accumulation of exhaustion that leads to long-term absence. Trials have recorded lower levels of stress and improved sleep, and companies report fewer short-term sick days. Healthier workers are not only more reliable but also more engaged, which further reduces the hidden costs of turnover and presenteeism.

Third, shortening the working week spreads available work across more people, easing unemployment and underemployment. In a labour market where automation and productivity gains concentrate tasks in fewer hands, a four-day week acts as a work-sharing mechanism. Rather than some employees logging 50 hours while others struggle to find any job, reducing the standard week creates demand for additional staff to cover hours and maintain services. This is especially valuable in sectors like healthcare, education, and retail, where demand cannot simply be compressed. More people earning wages also strengthens consumer spending and reduces welfare costs.

In short, the evidence from trials is clear: a four-day week delivers the same output, a healthier workforce, and a fairer distribution of work. National policy should catch up with what pioneering employers already know.

In an era where digital payments are increasingly ubiquitous, physical cash remains far more than a nostalgic relic; it is an essential pillar of a resilient, free, and inclusive economy. Its continued circulation safeguards societies against systemic fragility, preserves individual liberty, and protects those whom digital finance leaves behind.

The resilience of cash becomes most visible when infrastructure fails. Card terminals, mobile wallets, and online banking all depend on a continuous supply of electricity, functioning cellular networks, and stable data servers. During power outages, cyberattacks, natural disasters, or even routine network disruptions, digital payment systems can seize up without warning, leaving people unable to buy food, fuel, or medicine precisely when they need them most. Cash, by contrast, requires no authentication, no intermediary, and no signal. In the aftermath of a hurricane or a citywide blackout, a banknote still changes hands and completes a transaction instantly. This offline reliability makes cash not a competitor to digital payments but a vital backup that keeps commerce and emergency provisioning alive when the grid goes dark.

Cash also holds a unique position as the only widely available payment method that generates no transactional record. Every card swipe, mobile transfer, or online purchase leaves a data trail held by banks, payment processors, merchants, and sometimes governments. Those records can be aggregated, hacked, sold, or subpoenaed, turning private spending into a surveillance asset. Cash, in contrast, moves silently from hand to hand, creating no ledger of who paid whom, when, or for what. In a time of mass data collection and routine breaches, this anonymity protects not only personal privacy but also the freedom to make legal purchases—whether for political literature, health supplies, or charitable gifts—without being profiled. Cash preserves a sphere of economic life that remains outside observation.

Finally, robust cash circulation is indispensable for the unbanked and many elderly citizens. Millions of people lack bank accounts because of fees, documentation barriers, distrust, or poor credit history. Older adults, too, may struggle with smartphones, biometric authentication, or complex app interfaces, and they are frequent targets of digital fraud. For these groups, cash is not a preference but a necessity. It enables them to pay rent, buy groceries, and participate in daily commerce without a bank account or digital literacy. Removing or marginalising cash would deepen exclusion and force vulnerable people into dependence on others. Maintaining cash ensures that economic participation and dignity remain within everyone’s reach.

El trabajo a distancia debería convertirse en la modalidad habitual para los empleos de oficina, no como una excepción temporal, sino como una estrategia permanente de eficiencia y bienestar. Esta transformación beneficia tanto a los trabajadores como a las empresas, y sus ventajas son demasiado sólidas para ignorarlas.

En primer lugar, el tiempo que millones de personas pierden cada día en desplazamientos podría recuperarse para actividades productivas o personales. Quien pasa una o dos horas diarias en el tráfico o en el transporte público no solo llega cansado a su puesto, sino que ve reducidas sus horas de descanso, ejercicio o convivencia familiar. Si ese tiempo se invirtiera en adelantar tareas, formarse o simplemente descansar, la calidad de vida y la concentración laboral aumentarían de forma notable. Una persona que no empieza el día agotada por un trayecto largo rinde mejor y se siente más comprometida con su empleo.

Además, las empresas ganan acceso a un mercado de talento mucho más amplio. Cuando la presencia física diaria no es un requisito, la contratación deja de limitarse a quienes viven cerca de la oficina o están dispuestos a mudarse. Una compañía puede incorporar a un programador excelente en otra provincia, a una diseñadora en otro país o a un especialista en una zona rural, sin obligarlos a abandonar su entorno. Esta diversidad geográfica enriquece los equipos con perspectivas distintas y permite cubrir vacantes con los perfiles más cualificados, no solo con los más disponibles.

Por último, la reducción de los costes asociados al espacio de oficina libera recursos que pueden destinarse a salarios o a investigación. El alquiler, el mantenimiento, la electricidad y el mobiliario de grandes sedes representan una parte considerable del presupuesto de muchas organizaciones. Al adoptar el trabajo a distancia como norma, las empresas pueden reducir metros cuadrados y gastos fijos, y reinvertir ese dinero en mejorar la retribución de sus empleados o en proyectos de innovación. Así, el ahorro no se queda en un balance contable, sino que se traduce en equipos mejor pagados y en mayor capacidad competitiva.

En definitiva, el trabajo a distancia no es una renuncia a la productividad, sino una forma más inteligente de organizarla. Recuperar el tiempo de los desplazamientos, ampliar el acceso al talento y reducir costes innecesarios son razones suficientes para que esta modalidad deje de ser una alternativa y se convierta en la regla.

The proposal to phase out zoos is dangerously shortsighted, ignoring the irreplaceable contributions these institutions make to global conservation. Far from being outdated relics, modern accredited zoos are active forces for species survival, public engagement, and scientific advancement. Eliminating them would sever a lifeline for countless animals.

First, modern zoos operate sophisticated breeding programmes that have literally saved species from extinction. The Arabian oryx, once extinct in the wild, was restored through captive breeding initiated by zoos. Similarly, the California condor, black-footed ferret, and Przewalski's horse owe their continued existence to coordinated zoo-based efforts. These are not isolated successes; zoos maintain genetically viable insurance populations for hundreds of threatened species, providing a crucial buffer against habitat loss and poaching. Without these programmes, many animals would vanish forever.

Second, direct contact between the public and live animals is a powerful catalyst for conservation support. No documentary or photograph can replicate the emotional impact of standing face-to-face with a majestic tiger or a playful otter. This tangible encounter transforms abstract statistics about deforestation or climate change into personal concern for individual creatures. Studies consistently show that zoo visitors leave with increased awareness and willingness to support conservation financially and politically. By severing this direct connection, phasing out zoos would erode the very public empathy that funds and drives habitat protection worldwide.

Finally, veterinary research conducted in zoos yields profound benefits for wild animal populations. Zoo veterinarians develop anaesthetic protocols, diagnostic tools, and surgical techniques that are later applied in field conservation. For example, techniques for immobilising and treating wild elephants, rhinos, and big cats were refined in zoo settings. Research on zoo animals has advanced understanding of diseases like chytrid fungus in amphibians and white-nose syndrome in bats, enabling targeted interventions in the wild. This medical knowledge is directly transferable and often impossible to obtain from free-ranging animals that cannot be closely monitored.

In conclusion, phasing out zoos would not liberate animals; it would condemn many to extinction and strip humanity of the inspiration and expertise needed to protect them. We must champion modern zoos as essential partners in conservation, not dismantle them.

Banning private cars from city centres is not merely a transport adjustment but a fundamental reclaiming of public space. When private vehicles are removed, the vast acreage previously devoted to moving and storing cars—traffic lanes, parking bays, and queuing zones—can be reallocated to people. Wide, unobstructed pavements allow pedestrians to walk safely and comfortably, while dedicated cycle lanes encourage active travel without the constant threat of motor traffic. Former parking spaces become pocket parks, outdoor seating areas, market stalls, and restaurant terraces. This transformation turns streets from hostile corridors into vibrant public rooms where commercial and social life can flourish, making the city centre a destination rather than a place to pass through.

The environmental case is supported by strong empirical evidence of rapid improvement. Following the introduction of car bans or severe restrictions in cities such as Oslo, Madrid, and Brussels, monitoring stations recorded substantial falls in nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter, often within the first year. Noise pollution also drops markedly when engines and horns are removed; average daytime sound levels can fall by several decibels, which in urban acoustics represents a dramatic perceptual shift. These gains are not hypothetical or delayed—they emerge almost immediately as traffic volumes fall, demonstrating that the policy delivers measurable public health benefits in a short timeframe and making it one of the fastest available interventions for urban air quality.

Perhaps the most counterintuitive result is that retail footfall tends to rise, not fall, after private car access is restricted. The assumption that shoppers arrive primarily by car is repeatedly disproven: pedestrians and cyclists visit more often, stay longer, and spend more per square metre than drivers, who typically make single-destination trips and leave quickly. Cities that have pedestrianised central shopping streets, from Copenhagen to New York, have recorded increased footfall and sales. Freed from noise, fumes, and danger, streets become pleasant places to browse and linger, attracting families, tourists, and workers who otherwise would avoid congested thoroughfares. Thus, far from harming trade, removing private cars strengthens the economic vitality of the city centre.

En un mundo cada vez más interconectado, resulta paradójico que la norma predominante para millones de trabajadores de oficina siga siendo el desplazamiento diario hacia un lugar físico. La tecnología actual permite una comunicación fluida y una colaboración eficaz sin importar la distancia, por lo que el trabajo a distancia no debería ser una excepción temporal ni un beneficio ocasional, sino la modalidad habitual para los empleos administrativos. Adoptar este modelo de forma generalizada representa una triple victoria: para la calidad de vida del empleado, para la competitividad de la empresa y para la eficiencia económica del conjunto de la sociedad.

El primer beneficiario directo de esta transformación es el trabajador. El tiempo invertido en atascos o en transporte público congestionado es, en esencia, tiempo robado a la vida. Un trayecto medio de una hora al día suma más de 200 horas al año, el equivalente a varias semanas de vacaciones o a un curso de especialización completo. Al eliminar este desplazamiento, ese vasto capital temporal se reinvierte directamente en descanso reparador, en la preparación de comidas más saludables, en pasar tiempo con la familia o en el desarrollo personal y profesional. Esta flexibilidad no solo reduce el estrés y el agotamiento, sino que se traduce en un empleado más descansado, concentrado y, en última instancia, más productivo durante su jornada laboral efectiva.

Para las empresas, el cambio de mentalidad es igualmente estratégico. Cuando el requisito de presencialidad deja de ser un filtro, el acceso al talento se expande exponencialmente. Las compañías ya no se ven limitadas a contratar candidatos que vivan a una distancia razonable de sus oficinas, sino que pueden incorporar al mejor ingeniero, al creativo más brillante o al gestor más eficaz, sin importar si reside en otra ciudad, otra región o incluso otro país. Esta diversidad geográfica fomenta la innovación, aporta perspectivas culturales variadas y permite a las organizaciones operar en múltiples zonas horarias, atendiendo mejor a clientes globales. Además, este modelo es una poderosa herramienta de retención de talento, ya que muchos profesionales altamente cualificados priorizan la flexibilidad sobre otros beneficios.

Finalmente, existe un argumento económico incontestable. El mantenimiento de grandes sedes corporativas supone una sangría constante de recursos: alquileres elevados, facturas de suministros, mobiliario, limpieza y seguridad. Al reducir drásticamente la necesidad de espacio físico, las empresas liberan un capital considerable. Estos fondos pueden redirigirse estratégicamente hacia lo que realmente impulsa el crecimiento y la satisfacción laboral: aumentar los salarios de los empleados, que a su vez ven incrementado su poder adquisitivo al ahorrar en combustible o tarjetas de transporte, o invertir en investigación y desarrollo. En un entorno económico tan competitivo, desviar fondos del alquiler de metros cuadrados a la innovación o al capital humano es una decisión de pura inteligencia empresarial.

Las objeciones sobre la pérdida de la cultura corporativa o la dificultad de supervisión son superables con una gestión moderna basada en objetivos y en la comunicación deliberada. Los beneficios, en cambio, son tangibles y medibles. El trabajo a distancia no es una utopía, sino una evolución lógica y pragmática del entorno laboral. Es hora de que dejemos de valorar la presencia y empecemos a valorar la contribución. Adoptar el trabajo a distancia como norma no es solo una cuestión de comodidad; es una estrategia fundamental para construir una economía más humana, eficiente y competitiva.

En los últimos años, se ha abierto un intenso debate sobre la conveniencia de eliminar las tareas escolares en la educación primaria. Quienes proponen su supresión argumentan que reducen el estrés infantil y mejoran la calidad de vida de los alumnos. Sin embargo, considero que las tareas para casa, bien planificadas y en su justa medida, son una herramienta pedagógica valiosa en esta etapa. Mantenerlas no solo es beneficioso, sino necesario por tres razones fundamentales.

En primer lugar, las tareas escolares permiten consolidar los conocimientos adquiridos en el aula. Durante la jornada escolar, los niños reciben una gran cantidad de información nueva: aprenden a leer, a sumar, a comprender fenómenos naturales. Sin embargo, el aprendizaje no termina cuando suena el timbre. La práctica en casa, mediante ejercicios breves de lectura, escritura o cálculo, ayuda a fijar esos contenidos en la memoria a largo plazo. Por ejemplo, un niño que repasa en casa las tablas de multiplicar o lee diez minutos al día refuerza lo visto en clase y llega a la siguiente sesión con mayor seguridad. Sin esa práctica, muchos aprendizajes quedarían incompletos o se olvidarían rápidamente.

En segundo lugar, las tareas preparan a los alumnos para la educación secundaria. En esta etapa posterior, la carga de trabajo autónomo aumenta considerablemente: los estudiantes deben estudiar para exámenes, elaborar trabajos y gestionar varias asignaturas. Si en primaria no se han creado hábitos de estudio, responsabilidad y organización, el salto a secundaria puede resultar abrumador. Las tareas en primaria, aunque sean sencillas, enseñan a los niños a administrar su tiempo, a cumplir plazos y a esforzarse de manera constante. Un alumno que desde pequeño aprende a sentarse unos minutos cada tarde a repasar o completar una ficha, desarrolla una disciplina que le será imprescindible en el futuro académico.

En tercer lugar, las tareas escolares favorecen la implicación de los padres en el proceso de aprendizaje de sus hijos. Cuando un niño lleva una tarea a casa, se abre una ventana para que la familia conozca qué está aprendiendo, cuáles son sus fortalezas y en qué necesita ayuda. No se trata de que los padres hagan los deberes por ellos, sino de que acompañen, supervisen y muestren interés. Por ejemplo, leer juntos un cuento, revisar una suma o comentar un pequeño proyecto permite a los padres participar activamente en la educación de sus hijos y detectar a tiempo posibles dificultades. Esta colaboración entre escuela y familia refuerza el mensaje de que aprender es importante y crea un vínculo positivo con el conocimiento.

En conclusión, las tareas para casa en primaria no deben ser vistas como una carga innecesaria, sino como una oportunidad para afianzar lo aprendido, preparar a los alumnos para retos futuros e involucrar a las familias en la educación. Eso sí, siempre que sean razonables, adecuadas a la edad y no roben el tiempo necesario para el juego y el descanso. El equilibrio es la clave, pero eliminar por completo esta herramienta sería privar a los niños de un recurso valioso para su desarrollo académico y personal.

En el actual debate sobre la conveniencia de eliminar las tareas escolares en primaria, conviene no dejarse llevar solo por la búsqueda de una menor presión inmediata. Si bien es cierto que el exceso de deberes puede generar estrés, suprimirlos por completo supondría privar a los alumnos de una herramienta educativa de gran valor. Mantener unas tareas adecuadas y bien planificadas sigue siendo esencial por tres motivos fundamentales.

En primer lugar, las tareas para casa son clave para consolidar lo aprendido en clase. Durante la jornada escolar, el maestro explica conceptos nuevos, pero el tiempo para practicarlos es limitado. Unos ejercicios de matemáticas o una breve lectura por la tarde permiten que el niño repase, se equivoque y corrija en un entorno tranquilo. Esta práctica refuerza las conexiones neuronales y convierte un conocimiento frágil en un aprendizaje duradero. Sin esa repetición espaciada, muchos contenidos se olvidan rápidamente.

En segundo lugar, los deberes preparan a los estudiantes para la educación secundaria, donde la exigencia académica y la autonomía aumentan de forma considerable. Un niño que nunca ha tenido la responsabilidad de organizar su tiempo, apuntar sus tareas o completar un trabajo en casa llegará a primero de la ESO con una clara desventaja. Las tareas en primaria, si son razonables, sirven como un entrenamiento progresivo: enseñan a planificarse, a priorizar y a esforzarse de manera constante. Crean, en definitiva, un hábito de estudio que resulta imprescindible para el éxito futuro.

Por último, las tareas escolares ofrecen una oportunidad única para que los padres se impliquen en el proceso educativo de sus hijos. No se trata de que los adultos hagan los deberes, sino de que se sienten a su lado, les pregunten qué han aprendido y les ayuden a resolver dudas. Este momento compartido permite a las familias conocer las fortalezas y dificultades del niño, detectar problemas a tiempo y transmitir, con su actitud, que la educación es importante. La tarea actúa como un puente entre el colegio y el hogar, reforzando el mensaje de que ambos entornos colaboran en una misma dirección.

En conclusión, lejos de ser una carga innecesaria, las tareas para casa bien dosificadas consolidan el saber, forjan hábitos de trabajo y fortalecen el vínculo familia-escuela. Eliminarlas por completo no aliviaría el estrés, sino que generaría nuevas dificultades en el futuro. La solución no es suprimirlas, sino adaptarlas a la edad y a las necesidades reales de cada alumno.

El transporte público urbano gratuito no es un gasto, sino una inversión estratégica. Su gratuidad elimina barreras económicas y genera beneficios concretos en la operación, la movilidad y la equidad.

En primer lugar, suprimir el cobro de tarifas reduce significativamente los costos asociados a la recaudación. Los sistemas de boletería, validación, mantenimiento de máquinas, manejo de efectivo, control de evasión y personal dedicado a la venta representan una proporción considerable del presupuesto operativo. Al eliminar estos componentes, los recursos pueden redirigirse a mejorar frecuencias, ampliar cobertura y mantener la flota. Aunque se renuncia a los ingresos tarifarios, el ahorro administrativo y la simplificación del embarque compensan parcialmente esa pérdida y hacen más eficiente el servicio.

En segundo lugar, la gratuidad transforma los patrones de movilidad. Uno de los principales obstáculos para usar el transporte público es el costo directo, especialmente en viajes cortos donde el automóvil parece más conveniente. Al ser gratuito, el transporte colectivo compite con ventaja frente al vehículo privado. Muchos viajes cortos en automóvil —los que más congestión generan por su alta frecuencia y baja ocupación— pueden transferirse al bus o al metro. Menos autos en circulación reduce la congestión, el tiempo de viaje de todos y las emisiones contaminantes. Además, al aumentar la demanda peatonal y de transbordo, se dinamizan los centros urbanos y se desincentiva la expansión dispersa.

En tercer lugar, la gratuidad mejora la accesibilidad de los sectores de menores ingresos. El gasto en transporte suele ser regresivo: consume una mayor proporción del ingreso de los hogares pobres y limita su acceso a empleos lejanos, educación y salud. Eliminar la tarifa amplía efectivamente el área de búsqueda laboral y reduce el aislamiento territorial de barrios periféricos. Esto fortalece la inclusión social, disminuye la segregación y permite que las oportunidades no dependan de la capacidad de pago.

En suma, la gratuidad del transporte público urbano, financiada con impuestos progresivos y acompañada de inversión en capacidad, es una política transformadora para lograr ciudades más justas, eficientes y sostenibles.

**La energía nuclear como pilar imprescindible de la descarbonización eléctrica**

La descarbonización profunda del sector eléctrico no puede sustentarse exclusivamente en fuentes variables. La energía nuclear aporta una potencia firme y despachable, con factores de capacidad superiores al 90 % y una producción independiente de las condiciones meteorológicas. Esta cualidad complementa a la eólica y a la solar fotovoltaica: reduce la variabilidad residual del sistema, proporciona inercia síncrona y servicios de regulación de frecuencia, y disminuye los requerimientos de almacenamiento estacional y de respaldo fósil. En sistemas con alta penetración renovable, la base nuclear permite mantener la cobertura de la demanda durante periodos prolongados de baja disponibilidad eólica y solar, evitando la operación de ciclos combinados de gas como respaldo marginal.

En cuanto a las emisiones a lo largo del ciclo de vida, los análisis armonizados del IPCC sitúan la mediana nuclear en torno a 5-6 gCO₂eq/kWh, comparable a la eólica terrestre y marina, cuyas medianas oscilan entre 10 y 14 gCO₂eq/kWh, y muy por debajo de la solar fotovoltaica de gran escala y del gas natural. Estas cifras incorporan minería, enriquecimiento, construcción, operación, mantenimiento, desmantelamiento y gestión de residuos. Por tanto, la objeción de que la nuclear no es una fuente baja en carbono carece de sustento empírico: su intensidad de emisiones es del mismo orden que la eólica y hasta dos órdenes de magnitud inferior a la de las fuentes fósiles.

Finalmente, la eficiencia en el uso del suelo constituye una ventaja estratégica decisiva. La elevada densidad energética nuclear permite generar del orden de 1 TWh/año en pocas hectáreas, con una ocupación directa e indirecta estimada en torno a 0,1 m²/MWh, frente a varios m²/MWh de la eólica y decenas en el caso de la solar fotovoltaica. Esta menor huella territorial reduce los conflictos por uso de suelo, el impacto sobre ecosistemas y la necesidad de nuevas líneas de evacuación en áreas remotas.

Excluir la energía nuclear del mix descarbonizado obliga a sobredimensionar renovables, almacenamiento y redes, elevando costes y riesgos de suministro. Una cartera tecnológica que integre nuclear, eólica y solar es la vía más robusta, eficiente y ambientalmente racional hacia la neutralidad climática.

The case for teaching programming to all six-year-olds often appeals to a future-ready workforce, but it misunderstands how children learn and what schools can realistically deliver. Early coding mandates would divert time from more essential work and promise benefits that are largely illusory.

The first years of schooling should build a deep foundation in language, number sense, and imaginative play. At six, children need to hear rich stories, build vocabulary, play with quantities, and engage in pretend play that develops self-regulation and cooperation. These activities are not a delay of technical learning; they are its prerequisites. Programming demands abstract symbol manipulation and sequential reasoning. A child who cannot yet comfortably narrate a sequence of events or compare quantities will experience coding as meaningless symbol-shuffling. By contrast, a child grounded in language and number is far better prepared to learn computational thinking later.

The rapid churn of programming tools also undermines early instruction. The block-based apps or child-friendly robots used today may be obsolete or abandoned by the time a pupil reaches secondary school. Skills tied to a specific interface or platform have a short shelf life, and much of what is taught at age six is therefore transient. The lasting mental habits behind programming—breaking problems into parts, testing ideas, debugging—are better developed through puzzles, construction, and mathematics without pretending that young children are learning a future-proof technical skill.

Finally, there is a severe shortage of qualified teachers capable of delivering high-quality coding instruction. Most primary teachers have little or no computer science training. If coding becomes a universal requirement, schools will either rely on underprepared generalists or purchase superficial software that does the thinking for the child. Wealthier districts may hire specialists, while others offer a hollow version of the subject, widening inequality. A bad early encounter can also convince children that programming is boring or impossibly hard, discouraging them from pursuing it later.

Universal coding at six is an appealing slogan but poor educational policy. We should instead invest in foundational literacy, numeracy, play, and the long-term preparation of teachers.

La verificación obligatoria de la edad para acceder a redes sociales puede parecer una solución razonable para proteger a los menores, pero sus costos superan con creces sus posibles beneficios. Esta medida compromete derechos fundamentales, resulta fácil de eludir y profundiza desigualdades existentes.

En primer lugar, exige una intrusión desproporcionada en la privacidad de los usuarios. Para demostrar su edad, las personas tendrían que entregar documentos de identidad, datos biométricos o información bancaria a las plataformas. Esto crea enormes bases de datos centralizadas que se convierten en objetivos atractivos para ciberdelincuentes y pueden ser utilizadas para fines de vigilancia o perfiles comerciales no consentidos. La red dejaría de ser un espacio relativamente anónimo para transformarse en un entorno donde cada interacción está vinculada a una identidad verificada, lo que enfría la libertad de expresión y desalienta la participación de quienes temen represalias.

En segundo lugar, su efectividad para impedir el acceso de menores es altamente cuestionable. Los adolescentes con conocimientos técnicos básicos pueden recurrir a identificaciones falsas, credenciales de adultos o redes privadas virtuales para simular otra ubicación. Además, muchos menores simplemente migrarán a plataformas menos reguladas o a foros ocultos donde la supervisión es nula y los riesgos son mayores. La verificación obligatoria no educa ni fomenta un uso responsable; solo crea una falsa sensación de seguridad mientras desplaza el problema hacia espacios más difíciles de controlar.

Por último, la medida excluye a grupos vulnerables de la población. Personas mayores, migrantes sin documentación oficial, habitantes de zonas rurales con poco acceso a servicios de identificación o ciudadanos de bajos recursos que no poseen documentos digitales quedarían fuera de las redes sociales.
